task: Numbered standard ACL 10 must permit sources in 10.100.10.0/24. Add that source permit; use a wildcard, not a subnet mask.

teaching.hint: A standard ACL tests only the packet’s source address.
teaching.takeaway: The /24 wildcard compares the first three octets and ignores the last. This entry cannot restrict the destination or service; those requirements need an extended ACL.

task: Create or enter VTY-ADMINS as a named IPv4 ACL for a policy that only compares administrator source addresses. Choose the narrowest ACL type that fits.

teaching.hint: The policy needs no destination, protocol or port match.
teaching.takeaway: A named standard list provides source-only matching. Defining the list and adding permits still leaves a separate VTY attachment step; naming it VTY-ADMINS does not apply it.

task: Numbered extended ACL 101 must allow clients in 10.100.10.0/24 to initiate HTTPS to 10.100.20.20, with any client source port. Add the permit using numeric destination port 443.

teaching.hint: Place the service-port test after the server destination.
teaching.takeaway: A client normally chooses an ephemeral source port. Putting the 443 test after the source address would match the wrong side of the connection and miss ordinary HTTPS requests.

task: You are configuring R1’s client-facing Gi0/0. Client requests enter here and leave Gi0/1 toward the server. Attach the complete IPv4 ACL 101 so requests are checked before routing.

teaching.hint: Direction is relative to the selected router interface.
teaching.takeaway: Inbound on Gi0/0 evaluates the entering request. A server reply leaving Gi0/0 does not traverse that attachment, so the same list is not automatically a return-traffic filter.

task: Create or enter named ACL CLIENTS-IN. Its policy must distinguish client destinations and TCP service ports, so select the appropriate IPv4 ACL type.

teaching.hint: A name does not determine whether the list can match destinations and ports.
teaching.takeaway: Extended matching is required for this service-specific policy. A named standard list would still match only source addresses, regardless of how descriptive its name is.

task: CLIENTS-IN already has sequence 10 permitting the approved HTTP service to 10.100.20.20 and sequence 30 permitting other destinations. Add sequence 20 denying all other IPv4 traffic from 10.100.10.0/24 to that server.

teaching.hint: Choose a protocol match broad enough to include TCP, UDP and ICMP.
teaching.takeaway: This deny sits after the intended service exception and before the broad permit. Moving it above 10 would also block HTTP; omitting it would let the final permit admit unwanted server traffic.

task: In CLIENTS-IN, sequence 10 permits HTTP and sequence 20 denies other client traffic to 10.100.20.20. Add sequence 15 allowing only ICMP echo requests from 10.100.10.10 to that server.

teaching.hint: The narrow exception must be evaluated before the broader deny.
teaching.takeaway: The exception works because first-match processing reaches sequence 15 before 20. It permits echo requests from one host; it does not grant other clients access or automatically admit echo replies through another filter.

task: Inside a named extended ACL on IOS supporting sequence editing, sequence 20 is confirmed to be an obsolete broad permit. Remove only that entry while preserving all other rules and the attachment.

teaching.hint: Use the entry’s sequence in the current ACL submode.
teaching.takeaway: Deleting one sequence preserves the rest of the list. Inspect the resulting first-match order; deleting the entire referenced ACL would change far more than the requested exception.

task: In a new server-side named extended ACL, permit TCP from WEB 10.100.20.20 source port 80 to clients in 10.100.10.0/24 only when ACK or RST is set. Use numeric port 80 and no sequence number.

teaching.hint: For replies, the server’s service port is the source port.
teaching.takeaway: The source-port test follows WEB’s address, and established checks ACK or RST. This is not session tracking: a matching forged ACK can pass even without a prior client connection.

task: SSH and local login already work. You are on the intended VTY range, and standard ACL VTY-ADMINS already lists allowed management sources. Apply it to new incoming management sessions, leaving transit traffic unchanged.

teaching.hint: VTY session restrictions use a line command rather than an interface packet filter.
teaching.takeaway: The access class limits sources opening sessions to these lines. Authentication and SSH transport remain separate controls, and every available VTY range needs the intended restriction.

task: After controlled allowed and denied tests, display the configured ACL entries and supported match counters so you can compare their increments with the recorded baseline.

teaching.hint: Inspect effective entry order as well as counter changes.
teaching.takeaway: A matching counter shows that an entry saw matching traffic, not that the application completed. A zero delta can reflect an earlier match, the wrong attachment or traffic that never reached the list.

task: ACL 101 exists, but its counters do not change during client tests. On R1, inspect Gi0/0’s actual inbound and outbound IPv4 ACL attachments.

teaching.hint: Check the interface’s IPv4 details; list existence alone proves no attachment.
teaching.takeaway: Read the Inbound and Outgoing access list fields against the packet path. Correct entries in an unattached list, or a list in the opposite direction, do not enforce the intended request policy.
